newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss govt pensions can buy stocks, foreign bonds.
newsitem.headline: Swiss govt pensions can buy stocks, foreign bonds.

text.p: Swiss government pension funds, with invested assets estimated at close to 30 billion Swiss francs, may place some of their holdings in Swiss domestic shares and bonds in foreign currencies, the government said.
The government has also agreed to allow the funds to purchase foreign bonds denominated in Swiss francs, the government's main pension fund administrator said.

The step is planned to take effect from January 1, 1997. Bankers were still debating what impact it would have on financial markets. They noted only around one billion francs would be channeled into the new investment areas.

"In the new investment policy, it is planned to allow (investment in) listed Swiss shares, foreign bonds denominated in some foreign currencies, as well as some shares on Swiss real estate funds," the AHV agency said in a statement.
The fund had invested assets totaling 27.0 billion francs at the end of 1995.
It is foreseen that about two percent will be invested in Swiss shares, and two percent in bonds in foreign currencies, a top official at the agency said.
The decision is aimed at improving the returns from the AHV agency, which is the main part of Switzerland's "first pillar" of public-sector pension providers.

Swiss bankers said the government pension funds have had a highly conservative policy allowing investments in bonds and other fixed-income paper, but not shares. The total invested sum is roughly equal to one year's worth of benefit payouts.
The AHV said that direct investments in real estate would be avoided, primarily for administrative and liqudity reasons.
Bankers were still speculating on how the assets will be invested.

"It will remain to be seen where the money flows. Will it be in blue chips, or will they also try to invest in middle-sized and smaller firms?" said Graziano Lusenti, head of institutional investment at Geneva-based Robecco Bank (Suisse).
He said it was also unclear if the government pension funds would later be allowed to invest in foreign shares as well, noting that the capitalisation of the Swiss share market is relatively small.
